original: make the tone of this email a bit warmer
rewrite:
<role>You are an expert communications strategist with twenty years of experience in corporate, nonprofit and personal correspondence.</role>

<instructions>
Your task is to revise the tone of the email provided by the user so that it reads as warmer. Warmth here means the reader feels acknowledged, respected and valued, while the email keeps its original purpose, facts, requests and structure. Work through the following steps in order.

1. Read the entire email carefully and identify its purpose, its audience, the relationship between sender and recipient, and every request or commitment it contains.
2. Identify every sentence that reads as cold, abrupt, transactional, overly formal or impersonal, and note why it reads that way.
3. For each such sentence, write a warmer alternative that keeps the meaning exactly, adding acknowledgement of the reader, appreciation where it is genuine, and softer phrasing for requests.
4. Adjust the greeting and the sign-off so they match the warmer tone without becoming overly familiar for the relationship.
5. Read the whole revised email again and make sure the tone is consistent from start to finish, that nothing sounds forced or saccharine, and that no facts, dates, names, numbers or requests have changed.
6. Make sure the email is not noticeably longer than the original, and trim any added warmth that does not earn its place.
</instructions>

<examples>
<example><before>Send me the report by Friday.</before><after>Could you send me the report by Friday? It would really help me prepare for Monday.</after></example>
<example><before>Your request has been denied.</before><after>Thank you for your request. Unfortunately we are not able to approve it this time, and I am sorry for the disappointment.</after></example>
<example><before>See attached.</before><after>I have attached the file for you. Let me know if anything is unclear.</after></example>
<example><before>Meeting moved to 3pm.</before><after>Quick heads up: we have moved the meeting to 3pm. Thanks for your flexibility.</after></example>
<example><before>Noted.</before><after>Thanks for letting me know, I have made a note of it.</after></example>
</examples>

<output_format>
Return only the revised email, with its subject line if the original had one. Do not include commentary, explanations, a list of changes, or any text before or after the email. Preserve the original paragraph breaks, and keep any lists, links, signatures and attachment references exactly where they were in the original email so the sender can paste the result directly into their email client without further editing, reformatting or checking, and so the recipient receives a message that is clearly the same message, only warmer in tone, more considerate of the reader, and more pleasant to read from the opening line through to the closing line and signature.
</output_format>

<email>
Paste the email here.
</email>
why: What NOT to over-apply: a one-line ask needs a short clear prompt, not a tagged essay with five examples.
